latest.title: Solar is mainstream power. What does that mean for the energy industry’s future?
latest.notes: Howard Wenger, president of Nextpower, first got interested in solar power during the energy crisis of the 1970s. In his 42-year career in the industry, he has seen an astonishing transformation, as solar has moved from a niche technology for highly specialized applications to a core contributor to meeting electricity demand. In this special episode of Energy Gang from the RE+ conference in Las Vegas, he talks to host Ed Crooks about where the solar industry is now, and where it is going in the future. Nextpower is a company that provides systems for the solar and storage industries, including trackers, inverters, foundations and electrical balance of system. As Howard says, “everything but the panel for large scale solar power and everything but the battery cell for battery storage.” It is a big player in the industry, providing equipment for 30% of all the power installed in the US last year. The AI data-center buildout is pushing electricity demand sharply higher, often faster than utilities can deliver grid connections. That creates demand for behind-the-meter power, often as an interim step until a grid connection can be agreed, and solar and storage have a vital role to play. Howard says the debate is often not about solar and storage versus gas, but about how solar and storage and gas can be combined to provide the cleanest possible power as quickly as possible, with the availability and reliability that data center operators demand. Howard’s argument is that by combining trackers, inverters, foundations, wiring and software into an engineered package, Nextpower can reduce costs, raise output, speed construction and lower project risk. Charged up by rising electricity demand, the business is growing fast. In its capital markets day for investors, held shortly before Howard spoke to Ed, the company raised its target for 2030 revenues by almost 50%, from $5.2 billion to $7.5 billion. The discussion also goes into the impact of policy uncertainty on solar and storage. With the successes for Democrats in the US midterm elections, speculation has inevitably been on the rise about possible future expansions and extensions of tax credits for renewable energy. But not everyone in the industry is enthusiastic about that prospect. Howard says Nextpower would be comfortable without clean-energy incentives, if the playing field with fossil fuels were level. However, he adds, the import tariffs and other additional costs placed on solar and storage mean that continued support from tax credits is needed. Nextpower™ (Nasdaq: NXT) is addressing that complexity by bringing together solar power generation, energy storage, power conversion, data intelligence and lifecycle services in one integrated technology platform. Building on more than a decade of leadership in utility-scale solar tracking, Nextpower engineers, delivers and supports technologies that help developers, utilities, and asset owners build faster, generate more energy and reduce long-term risk. latest.title: Tim Gould on the IEA's World Energy Outlook in a Year of Energy Shocks
latest.notes: The global energy system is being reshaped by powerful forces all at once. The Iran war and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have caused the largest oil supply shock in history. War and geopolitical tensions more broadly are changing how countries think about energy security. The rise of artificial intelligence and data centers is forcing a reckoning around how much electricity the world is going to need, and how it will be sourced. Plus, energy affordability has become central to political debates, while countries face growing pressures to reduce carbon emissions to address climate change. Together, these forces are making the energy outlook much more uncertain with enormous implications for investment, for policy decisions, for climate change. That's the backdrop for this year's World Energy Outlook from the International Energy Agency. Published annually, the Outlook draws on data across fuels and technologies to explore possible futures for the global energy system and the choices that will shape them. This week host Jason Bordoff talks with Tim Gould, chief economist at the International Energy Agency. They talk about the key findings of this year's Outlook during this incredibly consequential year. They look at how countries are responding to the crisis, the coming wave of LNG, the staying power of coal, and why cooling — not just AI — is driving electricity demand globally. Tim co-leads the IEA's work on the World Energy Outlook which was released on Thursday, November 19. He joined the IEA in 2008 as a specialist on Russian and Caspian energy. Before that, he worked on European and Eurasian energy issues in Brussels. Credits: Hosted by Jason Bordoff, Bill Loveless, and Daniel Sternoff. Produced by Mary Catherine O'Connor, Dara Diamond, and Kyu Lee. Engineering by Gregory Vilfranc.

latest.title: [Episode #288] – Extending the Grid
latest.notes: For a century, the bulk power system has grown region by region, with much of it built to handle peaks in demand that happen for a subset of hours each year. The energy transition will certainly need a plan for new grid infrastructure, one that looks beyond its old boundaries, but can we also extend and enhance the current grid to get more out of it, given everything it has inherited? Guests on this show have brought a range of ideas about the grid of the future, and how it can support the energy transition in better ways than simply repeating the infrastructure of the past. In this episode of our energy transition documentary series, we look at visions of the future grid from Lorenzo Kristov, who pictured a grid built up in layers from local power systems, and Christopher Clack, who modeled a national grid network with high-voltage direct current (HVDC) lines between regions that could cut carbon emissions from electricity without raising its projected cost. Ideas like these have been under discussion at the national level in the US, this year perhaps more than ever. In March 2026, the US Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held a hearing on the “State of the Bulk Power System.” There, Liza Reed of the Niskanen Center cited research estimating that, on average, each extra gigawatt of transmission between regions could have been worth about $100 million annually over the past decade. Since then, the Senate has passed a version of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which would address barriers to siting interstate power lines. As electrification and new loads push demand higher, more renewable generation comes online, and existing infrastructure retires, the debate about our future grid is moving toward a point where critical decisions have to be made to shape the energy transition’s future. latest.title: The truth about data centers and electricity prices
latest.notes: This is a public episode. If you'd like to discuss this with other subscribers or get access to bonus episodes, visit www.volts.wtf/subscribe Are data centers raising everyone else’s electricity rates? The extremely unsatisfying answer is, it depends. A new report puts numbers on it: depending on circumstances, a large new load can cut other customers’ rates as much as 6 percent or raise them as much as 9 percent. latest.title: Grid utilization, explained
latest.notes: The grid is built to serve peaks on the hottest afternoon or coldest morning of the year. The rest of the time, much of that capacity is unused. So how do we use more of it to accommodate load growth? A growing coalition of experts argues that the US electric system has vast untapped potential, hidden in the underutilized infrastructure we’ve already built. And they’re pushing utilization as a resource that utilities can harness. This fall, that idea became concrete. Under a first-of-a-kind law, Virginia required its two biggest utilities to file utilization metrics with regulators. Supporters say it will provide more visibility into parts of the system that can accommodate more power, and change the way utilities plan and build. This week, a deep dive into the concept of utilization: how it works, why it matters, and where it fits into the growth of the grid. This conversation was recorded live at Latitude Media’s Flex Summit in Austin, Texas. Stephen sits down with Molly Knoll, a senior advisor at Align Energy Advisors; Ian Magruder, founder and executive director of the Utilize Coalition; and Zach Zimmerman, director of research at Grid Strategies. They discuss how utilization should be defined, reflect on lessons learned from Virginia, and explore critiques of the approach. Open Circuit is brought to you by EnergyHub. latest.title: Clean firm power’s next test: Can nuclear and geothermal scale economically?
latest.notes: Rising electricity demand, especially from AI and data centers, has brought nuclear and geothermal back into focus as sources of clean, firm power. But demand, corporate partnerships and policy support are not the same as projects delivering affordable electricity on time. The central question is whether both technologies can turn renewed momentum into repeatable deployment. Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie, is joined by Jenifer Shafer, professor of chemistry and Ben L. Fryrear Presidential Chair at Colorado School of Mines, and Anna Littlefield, Geothermal and Low Carbon Technologies Program Manager at the Payne Institute for Public Policy. They compare what is driving this moment and where the routes to scale diverge. On nuclear, uprates and restarts could add capacity sooner than new builds, while small modular reactors are more likely to arrive in the 2030s. Shafer explains how fuel recycling could improve fuel security and reduce the amount of material requiring disposal, but would not remove the need for a repository. Cost, safeguards and social license remain central challenges, while progress through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is a key signal to watch. Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat in deep rock beyond the limited areas served by conventional hydrothermal resources. Drilling and reservoir engineering have advanced, but the test now is whether projects can sustain heat flow economically over time while managing water loss, scaling, corrosion and reservoir performance. Littlefield points to power purchase agreements scheduled for the 2028 to 2030 period as an important test of delivery, not yet proof of scale. Colorado’s permitting and development efforts, including work to assess whether treated oil and gas produced water can support geothermal circulation, may offer lessons for other states. The technologies face different constraints: nuclear must address fuel, waste and project execution, while geothermal must prove durable reservoirs and manage water and induced-seismicity concerns. Both also depend on community trust. The guests argue that developers need to listen to local concerns and share monitoring data, rather than assume technical explanations alone will win support. Over the next five years, the clearest evidence will be projects that reach operation and perform as promised, alongside nuclear licensing progress and geothermal’s ability to deliver contracted power reliably. latest.title: 256. Survival of the Fittest: The New Rules of Renewable Investing - Nov26
latest.notes: The renewable energy landscape has changed dramatically over the past decade. In the 2010s, investors benefited from cheap financing, generous government support and power grids able to absorb renewable intermittency. Today, the industry faces curtailment, negative power prices, declining capture rates, the end of subsidy schemes and significantly higher interest rates. So how do you survive – and thrive – as a renewable energy investor in this new environment? While some players are facing financial distress, others have successfully adapted and are thriving. In this episode, Laurent and Gerard sit down with Jordi Francesch, Global Head Clean Energy at Nuveen Infrastructure. Nuveen, the asset management subsidiary of TIAA, oversees approximately $2.6 trillion in public and private assets. Its renewable energy platform brings together Glennmont Partners, acquired in 2021, and Greencoat, acquired through Schroders in 2026. Combined, they represent more than 20 GW of wind, solar and battery storage assets, potentially positioning Nuveen as a major player in the consolidation wave ahead. Jordi explains how the market has evolved and how Nuveen has adapted its investment and asset management strategies. We discuss power shaping, portfolio management, hedging and trading, as well as emerging opportunities across technologies and geographies. We also explore how banks have changed their approach to financing renewable assets and, finally, how AI is transforming the way these assets are procured, financed and managed. The renewable investment playbook has changed. This conversation is about understanding the new rules and learning how to thrive in the next chapter of the energy transition. latest.title: Yard Stick: What Climate Tech Founders Need to Know About Venture Capital
latest.notes: Raising venture capital is often presented as a series of milestones: find investors, close a seed round, raise a Series A, and keep scaling. But what happens when a company does all those things successfully—and yet the market was built for changes? Chris Tolles, co-founder & CEO of Yard Stick, joins Climate Rising to reflect on building and financing a soil carbon measurement company from its founding in 2020 through its decision to end commercial operations in 2026. Yard Stick successfully developed a technology to measure carbon content in agricultural soils, raised multiple venture rounds, attracted investors including corporate, climate, and conservation-focused capital, and secured significant U.S. government contracts. However, in 2025 roughly $20 million of Yard Stick’s USDA contracts were canceled. Chris was faced with tough decisions about how the company should move forward, and what to do with the potentially climate critical technology they had developed. Chris discusses how government funding helped de-risk Yard Stick’s earliest venture financing, what fundraising labels such as pre-seed and Series A actually mean, how founders should evaluate investors beyond the money they provide, and why investor relationships and alignment become especially important when companies face difficult decisions. The conversation also explores a fundamental tension in climate entrepreneurship: venture capital moves quickly, while natural systems—and the markets built around them—often do not.

latest.title: The Failed Pivot to Asia—and What Comes Next: A Conversation with Mira Rapp-Hooper and Zack Cooper
latest.notes: For almost two decades, the United States has struggled to settle on and commit to the right strategy in Asia in the face of a rising China. U.S. President Donald Trump’s second-term foreign policy has put the struggle in particularly stark relief—as seen in recent days with his visit to China, including a joint meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But the question about what U.S. foreign policy can and should aim to achieve in the region goes well beyond Trump. To explore that question, Dan Kurtz-Phelan brought together two regular Foreign Affairs authors who have shaped both the debate on American strategy in Asia and, in their time in government, the strategy itself. Mira Rapp-Hooper, now a fellow at the Brookings Institution, served as senior director for Indo-Pacific Strategy on President Joe Biden’s National Security Council. And Zack Cooper, a fellow at American Enterprise Institute, has served at the Pentagon and on President George W. Bush’s National Security Council. In their conversation—recorded on Friday, November 20—they discussed the Trump administration’s China policy and the bigger challenges ahead in the Indo-Pacific. You can find sources, transcripts, and more episodes of The Foreign Affairs Interview at https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/foreign-affairs-interview

latest.title: The Father of Realism and the Purpose of Power
latest.notes: This episode unpacks the legacy of Hans Morgenthau, the founder of modern realist thought in foreign policy, and what it can teach us about American power today. Host: James M. Lindsay , Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy, CFR Guest: David M. Sacks , Senior Fellow for Asia Studies, CFR We Discuss: How Hans Morgenthau's boyhood in Coburg—the first German town to elect the Nazis to a majority—watched the rule of law collapse around him and pushed him toward a worldview built around power rather than law. Why Morgenthau's first book, Scientific Man versus Power Politics , was eviscerated by reviewers yet remained the work he most prized. Morgenthau's clash with Henry Kissinger over Vietnam, which showed two realists reaching opposite conclusions. How realists decide what counts as a vital interest, and why Morgenthau criticized the Truman Doctrine. Whether China is a revisionist power, and what Morgenthau's realism would mean for U.S. strategy regarding Taiwan and the first island chain. What Morgenthau meant by defining American power as “a light to attract strangers, not a flame to spread throughout the world.” Whether the Trump administration's embrace of power politics reflects Morgenthau's realism or the misuse of power he warned against. Why Morgenthau argued that nuclear weapons had made the nation-state obsolete. Mentioned on the Episode: E. H. Carr, The Twenty Years' Crisis: 1919–1939 , Macmillan Hans J. Morgenthau, In Defense of the National Interest , Alfred A. Knopf Hans J. Morgenthau, Politics Among Nations: The Struggle for Power and Peace , Alfred A. Knopf Hans J. latest.title: What the rise of the far right means for Germany and Europe
latest.notes: Germany has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters since Russia’s full-scale invasion, but that support has become a wedge issue in German politics. The right-wing Alternative für Deutschland party, or AfD, has repeatedly called for an end to military support for Ukraine and a resumption of energy trade with Russia. As the AfD – and parties like it – gain influence in Europe, will support for Ukraine falter? Gideon speaks to Wolfgang Schmidt, who was in the German chancellor’s office under Olaf Scholz and oversaw Germany’s intelligence services, about the power of continuity in foreign policy, how Germany can adapt to new economic pressures, and why it’s too early to write Europe off. latest.title: What's the status of the leadership races across the UN system?
latest.notes: This week, we discussed the event that brought together seven candidates vying for the World Health Organization’s top job : the WHO inaugural candidates’ forum. The seven faced questions on everything from their core agendas to how they would set priorities under the agency’s tight budget constraints. We also break down our key takeaways from the exclusive interviews which Devex has been conducting with the contenders. On the topic of leadership, we take a close look at the race to lead the Food and Agriculture Organization . We discuss the candidates vying for the role; and with three nominees from the EU recommended by the block’s member states, the clock is ticking for Europe to unite around one candidate to lead the organization. Digging into these stories, and others, Devex Senior Editor Rumbi Chakamba sits down with reporters Jenny Lei Ravelo and Rebecca Holland for the latest episode of our weekly podcast series. In this sponsored spotlight segment, Devex Executive Vice President and Executive Editor Kate Warren sits down with Harriet Andrews, director of women and family health at PATH, to discuss findings from PATH’s Blind Spots Maternal Health Briefing 2026 (https://www.path.org/our-impact/resources/maternal-health-rd-gaps-a-test-of-african-health-system-resilience/). Despite sub-Saharan Africa accounting for roughly 70% of global maternal deaths, only about 1% of tracked global health research and development investment targets the primary drivers of maternal mortality and illness. Andrews breaks down what it takes to close this inequity gap — from integrating screening and management for maternal infections and risk factors into routine antenatal care in Ghana, to advancing African health sovereignty by investing in locally led research and health systems across a woman’s entire life course.

latest.title: Middle Powers Unite at the Halifax International Security Forum
latest.notes: One of the big questions on my mind heading into this year's Halifax International Security Forum in Nova Scotia was how the Democratic landslide in the midterm elections would shape discussions among leading security officials from Canada, the United States, and Europe. On the one hand, the forum once again lacks participation from senior American officials. Despite the presence of a bipartisan U.S. Senate delegation, no State Department or Pentagon officials are attending—a deliberate choice by the Trump administration. On the other hand, the Democrats' strong showing in the midterms could have sent a message to middle powers that Trump's political dominance is not necessarily enduring. So, are they preparing for the United States to return to a common security architecture, or are they following Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's lead and declaring the Trump era a "rupture" from which the world cannot return? Joining me for this special live edition of Global Dispatches is Justin Ling, a columnist for the Toronto Star and proprietor of the Bug-Eyed and Shameless Substack. We discuss the state of U.S.-Canada relations, the prospects for middle-power diplomacy, and other highlights from this year's Halifax International Security Forum.

latest.title: Who Should and Shouldn't Get Aid? With Stefan Dercon and Charles Kenny
latest.notes: CGD's Rachel Glennerster speaks with the University of Oxford's Stefan Dercon and CGD's Charles Kenny about how donors should weigh poverty, political commitment, and the potential for impact when deciding where aid goes; whether aid can support both economic transformation and essential services in the poorest countries; and what reforms to the World Bank's IDA funding and OECD aid eligibility rules could help make aid more effective.
